extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers interested in moral and aesthetic essays (19th-century Emersonian audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century moral/philosophical essay discussing standards of behavior, the ethics and aesthetics of gift-giving, and the salutary effects of nature; it articulates what counts as noble conduct, fitting gifts, and authentic engagement with the natural world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty of behavior / natural aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The creators of Fashion organize 'beauty of behavior.' The natural aristocracy consists of persons in whom 'heroic dispositions are native; with the love of beauty, the delight in society, and the power to embellish the passing day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson gives examples (Scipio, the Cid, Sir Philip Sidney, Washington) and contrasts this native aristocracy with the actual social aristocracy. He notes these persons are often not found in the established aristocracy and that their presence vindicates the theory of society that anticipates them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance originates from birth/genius, not mere breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegance comes of no breeding, but of birth. It must be genius which takes that direction: it must be not courteous, but courtesy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artificially learned manners (mere breeding) will fail; true high behavior is rare and must be native or the product of genius. Emerson contrasts Scott's 'costume' dialogue with Shakespeare's naturally great dialogue to illustrate the difference between acquired affectation and genuine manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful behavior outweighs beautiful form
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful form is better than a beautiful face; a beautiful behavior is better than a beautiful form: it gives a higher pleasure than statues or pictures; it is the finest of the fine arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson emphasizes original, commanding manners (not learned from convention) that protect and exhilarate others—examples include a man 'who carried the holiday in his eye' and could be 'free as Robin Hood, yet with the port of an emperor.' Such behavior is superior to mere physical beauty or dress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's instinctive role in discerning deportment
rubrics_metrics.description: Woman, with her instinct of behavior, instantly detects in man a love of trifles, any coldness or imbecility, or any want of the large, flowing, magnanimous deportment indispensable in public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson praises the American advantage in excelling 'in women' and trusts women's 'inspiring and musical nature' to show how they shall be served. He illustrates with poetic examples (Hafiz's Persian Lilla) of women who elevate others' behavior and social atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion and social prestige are local and relative
rubrics_metrics.description: What fashion values are plants which thrive in very confined localities; out of these precincts they go for nothing—of no use in the farm, forest, market, war, literary or scientific circle, at sea, in friendship, or in thought or virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For those distressed by exclusion from fashionable society, Emerson recommends practical remedies (e.g., changing residence). He argues that the apparent grandeur of fashion is shadowy and relative and that courage and virtue can open its gates.

rubrics_metrics.name: True honor springs from the heart of love, not fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything that is called fashion and courtesy humbles itself before the cause and fountain of honor, namely the heart of love. This royal blood conquers and expands all that approaches it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson contrasts superficial wealth with the 'rich heart'—true richness is the capacity to help and succor others regardless of station. He uses the example of Osman, a generous poor man, to show how a great heart outshines formal rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowers and fruits are always fitting gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Flowers and fruits are always fit presents; flowers assert that a ray of beauty outvalues utilities, and fruits are the flower of commodities and admit of fantastic values being attached to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson elaborates why these natural gifts please: flowers suggest beauty and attention, fruits imply a proportion between labor and reward (e.g., someone inviting you far and setting before you summer-fruit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity dictates appropriate common gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: For common gifts, necessity makes pertinences — if the man at the door has no shoes, you needn't consider whether you could procure him a paint-box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a recipient has an imperative need, choosing is easy and appropriate; supplying first wants is heroic in our condition of dependence, and necessity does everything well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best gift is a portion of thyself (gifts should reflect the giver)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only gift is a portion of thyself. Thou must bleed for me. The poet brings his poem; the shepherd, his lamb; the farmer, corn; the miner, a gem; the sailor, coral and shells; the painter, his picture; the girl, a handkerchief of her own sewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such gifts restore society to primary basis by conveying a man's biography. Gifts purchased in shops that do not represent the giver are 'cold lifeless' and appropriate only for kings or symbolic transactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifts can degrade the recipient; receiving is delicate
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the office of a man to receive gifts. We wish to be self-sustained; the hand that feeds us is in some danger of being bitten. We can receive anything from love, for that is receiving it from ourselves; but not from one who assumes to bestow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson notes the complex emotions of receiver (shame at dependence, embarrassment when gift reveals one's desires) and counsels sensitivity: giving that invades independence can produce humiliation or resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect gratitude; the expectation is mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The expectation of gratitude is mean, and is continually punished by the total insensibility of the obliged person. It is a great happiness to get off without injury and heart-burning from one who has had the ill-luck to be served by you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson approves the Buddhist maxim 'Do not flatter your benefactors.' He stresses the onerousness of serving for thanks and the superior moral posture of giving without expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifts should relate to the recipient's character
rubrics_metrics.description: One rule for a gift is that we might convey to some person that which properly belonged to his character, and was easily associated with him in thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This increases the meaningfulness of the present and ties it to the recipient's identity; it is preferable to arbitrary or purely ornamental presents that do not correspond to character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature as restorative, sobering, and ennobling
rubrics_metrics.description: There are days when the world reaches its perfection and nature's harmony (air, heavenly bodies, earth) makes us feel we have lived enough; such natural enchantments are medicinal—they sober and heal us and shame our religions and heroes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson describes the effects (temperament change, perspective, 'nestling in nature')—nature reduces the importance of social trifles, enhances taste, and makes a person 'hard to please' with superficial art; he cites Indian summer, woods, sunsets, and the musical wind as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine engagement with nature required; avoid dilettantism
rubrics_metrics.description: A dilettantism in nature is barren and unworthy; the 'fop of fields' is no better than his brother of Broadway. One who would truly honor nature must not be frivolous or merely fashionable about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson warns against euphuism and trivializing natural topics in mixed company; genuine humility and curiosity (carrying a plant, studying the land) are the right approaches to nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature is consistent and gradual—motion and rest
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature publishes itself in creatures through transformation on transformation to the highest symmetries; motion (change) and identity (rest) are her primary secrets—small motions over boundless time produce immense results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson draws on geology and organic development: formations arise by patient periods, and complexity (from rock to trilobite to man) follows slow laws. This is an evaluative framework for understanding natural processes and resisting short-sighted measures.
